summary.text: A liquid is a state of matter with a definite volume but no fixed shape, so it adapts to the shape of its container.
Its particles are held by bonds of intermediate strength, which let them move around one another while staying closely packed.
Liquids are nearly incompressible, so a pressure change at one point reaches every other part undiminished, which suits them to transmitting hydraulic power.

items.prompt: A mechanic presses the brake pedal and pushes on fluid in a sealed line. What happens to that push at the far end of the line?

options.label: It fades along the way, because the fluid squeezes down to soak it up
It arrives almost undiminished, because little energy goes into squeezing the fluid
It reaches only the nearest part of the fluid and stops there
It doubles, because the fluid stores the push and releases it

items.prompt: You heat a pot of water on the stove. What happens to the water molecules as it warms?

options.label: They vibrate harder and drift farther apart
They slow down and pack closer together

options.label: Tiny solid crystals that freeze out of the water and scrape it
Bubbles that form in low-pressure spots, then collapse with strong local force

options.label: Water is the only substance that can ever be a liquid
Most of the universe is solid rock, which leaves little room for liquid
They need a fairly narrow range of temperature and pressure to exist

paragraphs.heading: What a liquid is
paragraphs.text: A liquid is a state of matter that keeps a set volume but has no shape of its own. Pour it into a container and, under a force like gravity, it settles into the inside shape of that container in the direction the force pulls. It barely shrinks under pressure, holding on to its volume. Its density is usually near that of a solid and far above that of a gas. Liquids count as condensed matter, like solids, and as fluids, like gases.

paragraphs.heading: Between solid and gas
paragraphs.text: The atoms or molecules of a liquid are held together by intermolecular bonds of middling strength. These bonds let the particles slide around one another while still staying packed close. In a solid, much stronger forces lock the particles in place, so they can only jiggle slightly where they sit. In a gas, the particles are far apart, move freely and feel only weak forces from each other.

paragraphs.heading: Heating and cooling
paragraphs.text: Warm a liquid and its molecules vibrate harder, so the gaps between them grow. At the boiling point, the forces holding the molecules together can no longer keep them close, and the liquid turns into a gas. Cool it instead and the gaps shrink. At the freezing point the molecules usually line up in an orderly pattern, a process called crystallization, and the liquid becomes a solid. Liquid helium is the odd one out: at standard pressure it stays liquid even at absolute zero (0 K), because of its quantum properties.

paragraphs.heading: Rare in the universe
paragraphs.text: Liquid water is plentiful on Earth, yet liquid is the least common state of matter in the known universe. That is because a liquid can only exist within a fairly narrow band of temperature and pressure. Most known matter is gas, in interstellar clouds, or plasma, in stars. Only two elements, mercury and bromine, are liquid at standard temperature and pressure. Liquid water matters greatly in chemistry and biology and is needed by every known form of life.

paragraphs.heading: Hard to squeeze
paragraphs.text: Liquids can hardly be compressed at all. Each extra bar of pressure squeezes water by just 46.4 parts per million. Even at around 4000 bar at room temperature, water loses only 11% of its volume. That makes liquids good at carrying hydraulic power: push on one spot and the pressure change reaches every other part of the liquid at full strength, with very little energy wasted on squeezing it.

paragraphs.heading: Water hammer and cavitation
paragraphs.text: Being so hard to compress also leads to some striking effects. Shut a valve suddenly and a huge spike of pressure races back through the pipes at just under the speed of sound, making them bang; this is called water hammer. Liquids also have little give, so they can be torn apart where flow is very turbulent or turns sharply, such as at the back edge of a boat propeller or at a tight bend in a pipe. There, in the low pressure, the liquid turns to vapour and forms bubbles, which collapse once they reach higher pressure. The liquid then slams into the empty spaces with great local force and wears away nearby solid surfaces, an effect called cavitation.
